issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may interfere with a subordinate court’s order only on the jurisdictional or procedural grounds permitted by the revisional jurisdiction, and not merely because it would reach a different decision on the merits.
material_facts: A subordinate court continued a stay of compensation-apportionment proceedings pending an appeal from the dismissal of a specific-performance suit, reasoning that the appeal could affect apportionment.
The High Court, in revision, reversed that decision and directed continuation of the proceedings and payment of compensation.
The subordinate court had jurisdiction to make its order, and no illegality or material procedural irregularity in the manner it reached that order was established.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the limits of its revisional jurisdiction by treating the revision as if it were an appeal; its order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, clauses (a) and (b) concern exercise of jurisdiction not vested by law or failure to exercise jurisdiction so vested. Clause (c) concerns illegality or material irregularity in the manner of exercising jurisdiction, including breach of law or a material procedural defect affecting the decision; it does not permit correction of errors of fact or law in the decision itself once prescribed procedure has been followed. A different view on the merits does not justify revisional interference absent such a jurisdictional or procedural defect. The Court relied on Rajah Amir Hassan Khan v. Sheo Baksh Singh, 11 Indian Appeals 237; Balakrishna Udayar v. Vasudeva Aiyar, 44 Indian Appeals 261; and Keshav Deo v. Radha Kissan, [1953] S.C.R. 136.

rule.if: subordinate_order_reviewed_on_revision and subordinate_court_had_jurisdiction and no_jurisdictional_or_material_procedural_defect and high_court_reweighed_merits

predicates.subordinate_order_reviewed_on_revision: A higher court reviewed a subordinate court’s order in a revision proceeding.
predicates.subordinate_court_had_jurisdiction: The subordinate court had authority to decide the matter before it.
predicates.no_jurisdictional_or_material_procedural: The subordinate court neither exceeded nor failed to exercise its authority, and no material defect in its decision-making procedure was established.
predicates.high_court_reweighed_merits: The higher court changed the outcome because it preferred a different conclusion on the merits.

issues.definition: When a subordinate court had authority and no material jurisdictional or procedural defect is shown, a higher court acts improperly in revision if it changes the outcome merely because it would decide the merits differently.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not use an application for clarification to reverse a judicial order affecting another party without notice when the reversal should be pursued through an appeal or revision.
material_facts: After hearing both parties, the subordinate judge interpreted the High Court’s earlier order to mean that compensation would be paid only after the apportionment proceedings were decided.
The respondents applied to the High Court for clarification of its earlier order and referred to the subordinate judge’s interpretation.
The High Court made an order directing immediate payment without giving notice to the affected company, thereby effectively reversing the subordinate judge’s order.
issues.conclusion: The ex parte order was unsustainable; the challenge to the subordinate judge’s order should have been brought by an appropriate appeal or revision after notice to the affected party, not by an application for clarification.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 151 and 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not provide an appropriate basis, in these circumstances, to reverse the subordinate court’s judicial order. Such reversal should be sought through an appeal or revision after notice to the affected party. The Court cited no earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.clarification_application_used_to_challe: A party used an application seeking clarification to challenge a subordinate court’s order.
predicates.lower_court_order_made_after_hearing_par: The subordinate court made its order after hearing the parties affected by it.
predicates.higher_court_effectively_reversed_lower_: The higher court’s order changed the effect of the subordinate court’s judicial order.
predicates.affected_party_given_no_notice: The party affected by the reversal received no notice before the higher court made its order.

issues.definition: When a clarification application challenges an order made after hearing the parties, an effective reversal without notice to the affected party is unsustainable.
